title: Extracting functional trends from whole genome duplication events using comparative genomics
author: Hermansen, Hvidsten, et al.
materials: The process of gene duplication is believed to be a major factor in contributing to the generation of novel gene functions within a genome [10]. The process of small-scale (mostly tandem) gene duplication varies from the much larger but less common process of whole genome duplication (WGD). WGDs are believed to be mechanisms which allow for large species radiations and the introduction of novel biological pathways and survival strategies [11]. In the process of autopolyploid WGD, a complete copy of all genes and interacting partners is generated resulting in a doubling of the number of interacting partners in the genome. Immediately following the duplication, it is believed that all genes will retain their same function but will ultimately diverge in function or lose function. Furthermore during a WGD, there are no resulting partial or chimeric duplications as the entirety of the genome is duplicated. This reduces the complexity of determining the retention of the duplicated gene pairs as they are equally likely to be maintained or lost from the genome without having to account for differing evolutionary trajectories as the result of asymmetrical duplication [12–14].

The numerial trends in the conditional probabilities for the retention of the 3R and 4R WGD were similar for each of the five datasets suggesting that the quality controls used did not significantly change the results of the analysis. However the retention percentage of being retained at the 3R WGD and at the 4R WGD were lower when using the rigid phylogeny algorithm rather than the relaxed algorithm, suggesting that the relaxed algorithm did detect more retention of the 4R WGD. Furthermore there was a change in the fraction of interacting partners retained after the 4R WGD between the different datasets with dataset 1 showing a retention percentage of 74.98 % and dataset 5 having a retention percentage of 62.88 %. Each dataset was manually inspected and dataset 1 was used for the final analysis since it contained most genes, while still allowing for quality alignments and was able to detect the most WGDs at both the 3R and the 4R levels.

Although gene tree/species tree reconciliation can allow for some inference into the underlying evolutionary histories for gene families, current reconciliation programs rely on parsimony to minimize the number of inferred duplication and loss events within a gene tree. A more rigorous statistical framework has been developed to improve the inference of duplications through a birth/death model of gene retention as proposed by Arvestad et al. [44]. Extending the framework, Teufel et al. [56] and Zhao et al. [57] lay the foundation for assessing duplications based on time-heterogeneous birth/death models to make inference into the processes of duplication and loss using survival analysis. Explicit models for the time-dependent hazard of duplicates under neofunctionalization, subfunctionalization and dosage balance have been proposed [22, 56]. Furthermore it is important, when determining the evolutionary history of a gene, to be able to account for the population genetic dynamics that occur and the chance that a gene duplicate is lost not due to nonfunctionalization but simply due to not fixing within the population. The age-dependent expectation of this process has been described by Zhao et al. [57]. Together, these models provide a set of tools that can be used to make inference on mechanisms of duplicate gene retention in different genomes.

steps.title: Select species and outgroup
steps.instruction: Choose taxa that share the ancestral whole‑genome duplication (WGD) and closely related taxa without the WGD; designate a non‑WGD outgroup (e.g., spotted gar) for rooting gene trees.

steps.title: Generate gene families (BLAST all‑vs‑all)
steps.instruction: Run a BLAST all‑vs‑all on all protein sequences from the selected species, compute global PAM distances for each pair, and cluster homologous sequences into families using single‑linkage clustering.

steps.title: Add existing families and new sequences
steps.instruction: Import pre‑established families from databases such as Ensembl, TAED, and Selectome; add any missing sequences to these families with pplacer.

steps.title: Multiple sequence alignment
steps.instruction: Align each gene family using a progressive alignment program (MAFFT, MUSCLE, or PRANK).

steps.title: Model testing
steps.instruction: Determine the best substitution model for each protein alignment using Prottest or an equivalent model‑testing tool.

steps.title: Phylogenetic tree reconstruction
steps.instruction: Reconstruct a gene tree for each family with either Maximum Likelihood (PhyML) or Bayesian inference (MrBayes).

steps.title: Assess tree support
steps.instruction: Perform bootstrap analysis (for ML) or compute posterior probabilities (for Bayesian) and assign support values to every node.

steps.title: Gene‑tree/species‑tree reconciliation
steps.instruction: Reconcile each gene tree with the species tree using a parsimony‑based algorithm that minimizes duplication and loss events; for Atlantic salmon, use Softparsmap to place the minimal number of duplications and to enforce a speciation root with spotted gar as outgroup.

steps.title: Assign WGD categories to duplication nodes
steps.instruction: Map each duplication node onto the species tree and classify it as 3R, 4R, post‑3R‑pre‑4R, or post‑4R based on its position relative to the known WGD events.

substeps.instruction: If a node is ambiguous, examine chromosomal locations: duplicates on the same chromosome suggest a tandem (small‑scale) duplication, while duplicates on different chromosomes support a WGD classification.
When ambiguity remains, apply the heuristic: if a more ancient WGD node exists on the same lineage, label the ambiguous node as a small‑scale duplication; otherwise label it as a WGD.

steps.title: Examine and refine WGD locations
steps.instruction: In trees where no WGD was initially detected, re‑evaluate topology, presence of other WGDs, and chromosome locations; re‑assign nodes as WGDs when duplicates reside on different chromosomes and the topology permits.

steps.title: Classify duplication events against expectations
steps.instruction: For each WGD, expect a doubling of gene copies (2× after 3R, 4× after 4R). Compare observed copy numbers to these expectations; discrepancies indicate loss events or lineage‑specific small‑scale duplications.

steps.title: Calculate retention rates and statistical significance
steps.instruction: Count retained duplicates for each WGD, compute conditional probabilities of retention, and test differences with a pooled two‑proportion Z‑test (p‑values as in the original analysis).

steps.title: Construct multiple gene‑family datasets
steps.instruction: Create five datasets varying thresholds and phylogeny‑flexibility:

substeps.instruction: 1) Relaxed phylogeny, ≥50 % pairwise identity, no gap‑fraction threshold.

steps.title: Select final dataset for analysis
steps.instruction: Choose dataset 1 (relaxed phylogeny, 50 % identity, no gap threshold) because it retained the most genes while still providing quality alignments and detected the most WGDs.

steps.title: Retrieve protein‑protein interaction data
steps.instruction: Download interaction data from the STRING database (≥2000 species). If the target species is absent, select a phylogenetically similar species, perform a BLAST all‑against‑all to map homologs, and retain only interactions annotated as “binding”.

steps.title: Determine co‑retention of interacting partners
steps.instruction: For each gene, assess whether it is retained at a given WGD and whether each of its STRING‑identified interacting partners is also retained at the same WGD; compute conditional probabilities of co‑retention analogous to the single‑gene retention calculation.

steps.title: Analyze expression divergence of 4R duplicates
steps.instruction: Use an Atlantic salmon expression atlas covering 15 tissues:

substeps.instruction: Cluster genes into co‑expression groups; 45 % of duplicates fall into different clusters (diverged).
For each of the 8 102 salmon‑pike triplets, compute Pearson correlation between each salmon duplicate and the pike ortholog; 70 % show a significant correlation (p ≤ 0.05).
Classify a duplicate pair as neofunctionalized when only one salmon gene correlates with pike (p ≤ 0.05) while the sum of the two salmon genes correlates more strongly (p < 0.03).

steps.title: Access supplementary code and pseudocode
steps.instruction: Download the analysis pseudocode (Additional file 1) from https://liberles.cst.temple.edu/public/BPO/Hermansen_et_al_2016_additional_file_1.pdf and the custom Perl scripts from http://liberles.cst.temple.edu/public/Salmon_Genome_Project/.
